li.a: JSTOR Daily: How a Murder Fueled Racial Terror in Florida
Valdosta Daily Times: Lynching linked to Valdosta marks centennial (2022)
Equal Justice Initiative: On Dec 12, 1922, White Mob Lynches Arthur Young in Taylor County, Florida (archived copy)
TalkAfricana: Perry Massacre: How a Manhunt Turned Into Violence Against Black Families in Florida in 1922
Dreams of Black Wall Street: S2 E6 Perry, FL: One Month Before the Rosewood Massacre

content.p: In the first two weeks of December 1922, the small town of Perry, Florida, was swept by a manhunt, two lynchings and a burning of the Black neighborhood. The violence followed the killing of a white schoolteacher, Annie "Ruby" Hendry. Her death set off a chain of events that, in the words of the Valdosta Daily Times, is sometimes called the "Perry Massacre." Accounts of the case still disagree about how many people were killed and how the manhunt was organized, and the accounts that survive were shaped by the newspapers of the day.

Hendry's body was found on 2 December 1922. JSTOR Daily says her remains lay in tall grass beside a train track in Perry. The Valdosta Daily Times, drawing on a 2008 Florida State University thesis by Meghan H. Martinez, says a freight train crew found her near a creek. The Valdosta Daily Times, citing Martinez, says she was struck with a blunt tool and that her throat was cut, and that $14 had been taken from her. TalkAfricana also says she was beaten and her throat cut.

Hendry was a schoolteacher in the county seat, and her death frightened the white community. The Equal Justice Initiative says that items found near her body belonged to a local white man, but that police insisted the killer had to be a Black man and quickly focused on Charles Wright. Within days the search had become a campaign against Perry's Black residents as a whole.

JSTOR Daily reports that police arrested four local Black men the day after the body was found, although the officers had no meaningful clues. The Valdosta Daily Times says that on 5 December police named Wright, a Black sawmill operator, and said the murder weapons could be linked to him. JSTOR Daily describes the same man as an "escaped convict" from nearby Dixie County, and TalkAfricana describes him as a 21-year-old who had been living under an assumed name and says a shotgun and a razor found near the scene were linked to him. The sources do not agree on his occupation or his age. JSTOR Daily, summarizing historian Christopher Calton, says police never made public any evidence tying Wright to the killing.

According to the Valdosta Daily Times, more than 300 residents of Taylor and Madison counties joined posses hunting for Wright, and set guards on the county entrances. The Bristol Herald-Courier reported on 8 December that Sheriff Forrest Lipscomb of Taylor County was heading to Valdosta, Georgia, with a party of about 150 men and bloodhounds. The search reached as far as Georgia, and the Valdosta Daily Times reports that Young had been taken in the area of Kindalou, Georgia, and was described in the papers as a 30-year-old Black man and escaped convict.
content.h2: Dixie County and the meaning of "escaped convict"
content.p: Calton, as JSTOR Daily summarizes him, argues that the phrase "escaped convict" carried a specific meaning in rural Florida. It described a Black man forced by the convict leasing system into labor at an isolated turpentine camp. The county was new: it had been set up only the year before on a nearly uninhabited tract held by the Putnam Lumber Company. A local court there could send prisoners to lumber and turpentine camps. Men were often held through debt peonage, which, in JSTOR Daily's words, could change a three-month sentence into a lifetime of enslavement.

JSTOR Daily gives the background to the violence as well. When a new sawmill began hiring in 1913, its owners drew skilled hands from Louisiana, and the influx included Black workers who almost trebled Perry's Black residents. Laura Scott Reaves, who had been a child during the manhunt, gave Calton her memories, and she recalled that white men in Perry, struggling after the war's economic downturn, resented Black foremen. Calton's view, as JSTOR Daily reports it, is that the manhunt was a campaign of terror shaped by these economic and social pressures. He also writes that it is "impossible to identify how much of the violence stemmed from a culture of racism and notions of honor and how much, if any, was motivated by labor tensions in a depressed economy."

JSTOR Daily says that vigilantes menaced the homes of Black residents who were suspected of sheltering Wright, and that they killed a number of Black residents, reportedly including children. It describes one building burned each night that Wright remained at large, including the community's church, school, Masonic lodge and amusement hall. The Valdosta Daily Times says that two self-styled guards at the county lines killed a Black man who was unconnected with the manhunt, believing that he was pulling a gun on them. TalkAfricana describes a killing on 6 December, in which armed men stopped a Black traveller named Cubrit Dixon and shot him after he appeared to reach into his pocket. According to TalkAfricana, the men found only a closed pocketknife on him. The two accounts do not say whether this was the same incident.

The Valdosta Daily Times also reports that another Black man was shot and his house burned after he was accused of writing an "improper note" to a white woman. TalkAfricana dates that killing to 15 December. Dozens of Black families fled Perry and many did not return, according to the Equal Justice Initiative and TalkAfricana.

The Valdosta Daily Times says that a mob took Young to the Lowndes County jail in Georgia, and that he was moved in the night to the jail in Madison, Florida. The same account says Wright had been apprehended in Madison County. On 8 December Sheriff Lipscomb tried to move both men to the jail in Perry, but the party was overtaken by a mob that the 2008 thesis puts between 3,000 and 5,000 strong, drawn from the north of Florida and the south of Georgia. According to the thesis, both men were "given an audience" and a chance to confess. Wright reportedly admitted killing Hendry but said that Young had nothing to do with it. TalkAfricana says Wright was subjected to torture before he was killed, and that he maintained he had acted alone. These claims rest on the newspapers of the day and on later historians, and the sources do not give a court's finding on them.

JSTOR Daily says the mob chained Wright to a wooden stake and set him on fire. The Macon Daily Telegraph's report of 9 December, quoted by the Valdosta Daily Times, carried the headline "Charlie Wright, Alleged Slayer, Burns At Stake." Both the Equal Justice Initiative and TalkAfricana describe the killing as a public spectacle, and the Equal Justice Initiative says that the lynching was meant to terrorize the entire Black community as well as to harm Wright.

On 12 December the authorities tried again to secure Young. The Valdosta Daily Times says that Governor Cary Hardee, who came from Perry, ordered the sheriff to take Young to a jail beyond Taylor County for safekeeping. A smaller crowd overpowered the sheriff on the road towards Madison and took Young from his custody. The Macon News reported on 13 December that he had been shot and his body left hanging from a tree about seven miles from Perry. The newspaper quoted the sheriff as saying only that he had been overpowered on the road and that Young had been taken.

The Equal Justice Initiative says the mob riddled Young's body with bullets and left it hanging from a tree beside a highway in Perry. TalkAfricana gives the same account. The Valdosta Daily Times notes that the press of the day routinely called Young and Wright "negroes" in their articles and often assumed they were guilty, although neither man ever stood trial.

The accounts do not agree on several points, and they should be read together rather than as a single record. The number of people killed is the most important of these. The Valdosta Daily Times says four Black residents died during the violence. The Equal Justice Initiative counts two lynched men, Wright and Young, and says a mob of more than 1,000 people lynched them in Taylor County. JSTOR Daily says the vigilantes killed a number of Black residents, reportedly including children, without giving a count. TalkAfricana says white mobs killed several Black men. These counts do not agree with one another, and the Valdosta Daily Times says that tracking the details of the case is difficult.

The dates also differ. TalkAfricana puts Wright's killing on 8 December and Young's on 12 December, as the Valdosta Daily Times does. The Equal Justice Initiative does not give a date for Wright's death, and the Macon Daily Telegraph's report of the burning, quoted by the Valdosta Daily Times, appeared in its 9 December issue. The sources also differ on where Hendry's body was found, and on whether the Dixon killing was linked to the manhunt.

No one was prosecuted for either lynching, according to the Equal Justice Initiative and TalkAfricana. The Equal Justice Initiative lists Wright and Young among 15 documented African American victims of racial terror lynching in Taylor County between 1877 and 1950. TalkAfricana notes that the Perry events came two years after the Ocoee massacre in central Florida, and about a month before white mobs attacked the Black community of Rosewood. A podcast episode on Perry, which quotes Martinez and features a talk by Paul Ortiz, says the Perry violence could be viewed as a foreshadowing of Rosewood, and it places such incidents within the wider pattern of racial violence in early 20th-century Florida.

TalkAfricana observes that the Perry killings were less remembered in later decades than Ocoee or Rosewood. The Valdosta Daily Times notes that its own local newspaper files for mid-1922 to 1925 are missing, which makes the local record harder to reconstruct. Dozens of Black families who left Perry lost their homes, businesses and institutions, and those who remained knew what had happened to Wright and Young.
